source.title: Low-resourced languages get jailbroken more. Can SAEs explain why?

page_placements.theme: Multilingual and prompt-framing transfer: harm separation and direction-based interventions weaken in non-English and low-resource languages

record.tranche_reason: It tests cross-language transfer of refusal-associated features using correlations and one-feature logistic models, rather than the original difference-in-means direction and causal interventions.
record.gate_note: The study tests whether English refusal-associated SAE features retain their association across languages. It also reports refusal-rate contrasts before and after jailbreak prompts; those results concern language-specific jailbreak behavior, not whether a refusal direction carries across languages, so they are recorded under fits_no_version. It does not ablate, add, or causally intervene on the features.
record.test_reason: The study correlates individual Gemma-2-2B-IT SAE latents with refusal labels in English, Japanese, Spanish and Dutch. It never computes a harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction, and it never ablates, adds or steers anything. Sign flips in single sparse features are a related but different construct, because a distributed refusal direction could still transfer while individual latents drift. So it does not test V6 or any other version. Its findings go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The author concludes that English refusal-correlated SAE neurons lose predictive power or flip direction in other languages. That undermines the 'distractor' explanation and suggests limits on using SAEs for cross-lingual jailbreak interpretation.
record.recipe_differences: Measures refusal associations of SAE features using correlations and one-feature logistic models; it does not find the original harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction or intervene on it.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported feature associations vary by language; Japanese shows the strongest attenuation. Refusal-rate contrasts also differ between pre-jailbreak and post-jailbreak prompts.

fits_no_version.finding: In Gemma-2-2B-IT final-layer SAE, latents selected as refusal-correlated in English mostly lose significance in Japanese, Spanish and Dutch, and some flip sign. Feature #14018 has β=+0.979 in English and β=−0.787 in Japanese. The evidence is correlational only; there is no causal test.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Individual SAE latents correlated with refusal in one language do not keep that association in other languages.

fits_no_version.finding: Pre-jailbreak, English refusal rates are significantly higher than Spanish, Japanese and Dutch (p<0.05). Post-jailbreak the gaps shrink and are non-significant (p=0.55, 0.24, 0.27).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For this model and prompt set, language differences in refusal rates are larger before than after jailbreak tailoring.

record.problems: Only Gemma-2-2B-IT and the final SAE layer are studied; the text describes the exact feature as both final-layer and layer-12 residual. The translations were not human-verified, responses were limited to 30 tokens and judged by gpt-4o-mini, and exact refusal rates and most feature-level values are not provided. The article itself identifies limited time and uncertain generalization to larger models; it reports no ablation or steering validation.

untested.parts: Whether a difference-in-means refusal direction (or its ablation or addition effect) carries across languages, model variants, or from base to instruct. The study tests only correlations of individual SAE latents.
No direction extraction, ablation or addition.
Jailbreak prompts are used, but direction suppression is not measured.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 'challenges' label is withdrawn: SAE-latent correlation is not the refusal direction, and no intervention was run. Other caveats: a single 2B model; machine translations not checked by a human; 30-token responses judged by gpt-4o-mini. A commenter suggests the Japanese sign flip may come from polite preambles truncated before the refusal. The layer is inconsistently given as final versus layer 12.

versions.untested_parts: No difference-in-means direction is found and causally ablated or added; preservation of other abilities is not tested.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration is tested.
Jailbreak prompts are evaluated, but the study does not test whether attacks suppress a refusal direction or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
The study does not compare single-direction, affine, cone, or multiple-direction accounts.
The study does not separate harmfulness judgments from refusal decisions.

Tests language transfer of refusal-associated SAE features in one instruct model; it does not test the original difference-in-means direction, transfer across model variants, or transfer from base to instruct models.
No refusal-training method or training stage is varied.

relation.reason: The post discusses refusal features and cross-lingual refusal stability but neither cites nor uses the difference-in-means refusal direction. A refusal direction comes up only in a reader comment.

tranche.reason: The study correlates single Gemma-2-2B-IT SAE latents with judged refusal across languages. It never computes the harmful-minus-harmless direction or intervenes on anything. That is a related but different construct, so it does not test V6 or any other version; ablation and steering appear only as future work.

source_check.notes: The scatter's non-English points were themselves selected as non-significant ('I selected non-English points that fall to the right of it'), on top of English-significance selection, which favours regression to the mean. The p-values likely come from the one-sided correlation test. The judge is gpt-4o-mini on 30-token responses, and a commenter flags judge and truncation confounds. Post-jailbreak, the English vs other-language refusal gaps were non-significant (p=0.55, 0.24, 0.27).

statements.problem: No error. One caveat: the text names #14018's layer both 'final-layer' and 'layer-12 residual'. Also, the claim that latents 'mostly lose significance' is the author's aggregate wording; no per-language counts are given.
